title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Mobile massage
audience: Solo mobile massage therapists who want more sessions from clients that suit their service, their suburbs and their session length.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, session length and repeat need
Identify public signals that a need may be starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the sessions you do well, such as a 60-minute massage at the client’s home, and the 90-minute session if you offer it. Then write the price you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A regular session on a route you already run is worth more to a mobile therapist than a single session across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good prospect from a poor one. Describe the sessions you give, not any health benefit.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits in your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who books, and whether the session falls within your training, registration and insurance. The research found no verified route for mobile massage to venues, referrals or aged care, so treat each segment as a hypothesis to test. Segments to test include households already in your postcodes, workplaces with several staff, and local business networks that trade referrals between members; a Wyndham City Council directory lists such networks. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Keep only business contact details published for business use, and keep the list secure. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists. ACMA’s guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals, where they fit
instruction.body: A public signal is an event that makes a need more likely. Some councils publish a planning permit register with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register in Victoria’s open data portal. A register shows building projects, not demand for massage, so use it only to decide where to test. Government tender portals, such as Buying for Victoria and AusTender, list purchases, but the research found no tender for these sessions, so check before you rely on them. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, enter private property or call at a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you learned about the business or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business’s own published material. It then offers one small next step, such as a written price for a defined session or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know and make it simple to say no. Do not select or describe prospects by any health condition. Health information is sensitive, and the research did not cover the rules for using it in marketing, so do not use it without advice. The ACCC’s 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves, so a specific and honest message that names you is a practical advantage.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. The research sets no number, so choose one and record it. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid sessions, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the session, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call Register and your training and registration rules before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile massage therapist covers three suburbs. A council notice shows planned works at a building in one of them, and the building manager’s business email address is published on the building’s contact page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the therapist send a sales message to the manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The therapist should not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA’s guidance says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the therapist first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. The planned works are not a clear need for massage, so the therapist treats the building as a hypothesis, not a lead. If the manager has invited contact, one message names the notice, says how the business learned of it and offers one specific item, such as a written price for a defined session. A phone call to a number on the Do Not Call Register is limited by its rules, so the therapist checks the register first. The therapist does not contact individual residents or enter the common area.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, session length and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any home session follows the client’s access rules and your own hygiene routine

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private or health information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose, and do not select anyone by a health condition.

commonErrors.error: Offering a session that you are not trained, registered or insured to deliver in the state where it happens.
commonErrors.prevention: Check your training, registration and insurance before outreach, and remove any service you do not hold from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed, registered or authorised service in outreach unless you hold what the state or territory where the work is done requires. For massage, council registration in Victoria was not confirmed, and registration and council checks were not verified for other states and territories. Check the rule for each place you work. Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA’s avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA’s Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Telephone outreach: check the Do Not Call Register before calling. The DNCR guide (2018 copyright notice) says telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm, Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays. Public information does not by itself permit contact. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC’s direct-marketing guidance says public information is not exempt from its rules.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private or health information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private or health information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off session well outside your service area, because it looks large
A group of clients with several sessions inside your service area that you already see
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

Gaps: no verified route for mobile massage to reach venues, referrals or aged care; no source found that any prospect segment buys mobile massage; the Privacy Act coverage of small businesses and the rules for health information in marketing are not confirmed; the Spam Act 2003 text was not read; massage registration rules were not verified for most states.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include an unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Does not name the Spam Act 2003. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: APP 7 direct marketing (OAIC)
officialReferences.pageDate: page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019
officialReferences.covers: States that public information does not by itself exempt direct marketing from the rules. Publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.
